utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Zepinic. How are you today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to keep things as short as possible so could you please tell us, how long have you and I known each other? Not how long we've known of each other, but how long we've known each other personally?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that you're asking me, I know of you since the student demonstrations of 1968 and the speech that you made at the pavilion. By the way, you recited Njegus on the occasion. We've known each other since you were in power. Of course we knew each other from before from various gatherings. Inter alia, I think we attended an international conference of psychotherapists in Dubrovnik. Once you came to power it was only natural that we got to know each other better. Unfortunately, the role that was given to me as the top man of the Ministry of the Interior meant that through your files I found out a lot of details about all of you, your mentality, your nature, your personality, if you will. Since you've asked. It is only natural that I was interested in learning about your personality for professional reasons. I know that you were also involved in psychotherapy as I was. And I can tell you and conclude on that note, in many situations - as can be seen from the telephone conversations between the two of us - I did not see, or rather, I did not perceive Dr. Karadzic the way I knew him personally, as a person. Because in most of these cases, as you've probably seen through these transcripts, you used swear words, threats, bad language. Knowing you personally and having had coffee with you and having chatted with you, your nature is quite different and also that would not be the nature of a professional, a psychotherapist and a psychiatrist. So now that you're asking me, I can tell you that I knew two personalities: Dr. Karadzic as a professional, a family man, and so on; and Radovan Karadzic as president of the SDS, who was a bit the opposite of the Dr. Karadzic that I knew. Things were similar in relation to Alija Izetbegovic too. I don't know whether this has satisfied you in terms of an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not catch Mr. Karadzic's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said thank you. And as a matter of fact you forced out some of my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since we had a professional relationship, was our relationship very dynamic, sometimes even very sharp; and if so, why, on the basis of what, and that can be seen from the intercepts too?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Dr. Karadzic, these were bad times for our country and bad times for you and for me. By the very nature of things, regardless of our good relations, our good personal relations, in a way we were on two completely opposite sides, if I can put it that way. On one side I was there with my Ministry of the Interior working for coexistence in peace at all costs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and thereby peace in the territory throughout Yugoslavia, in the territory of all of Yugoslavia. Once the problem of Bosnia's resolved, the problem of the former Yugoslavia would be resolved, or rather, the problem of the Balkans. On the other hand, you were a member of the coalition force that was given the mandate to set up a government, and you included me in that government. This coalition had a very optimistic view and made quite a few promises to Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, nothing came out of that. This coalition, it's not that it never functioned as a coalition. As a matter of fact, on the inside, so it's not only that you clashed with those who were against the coalition, but even you as coalition partners had such divergent relations that the only question was for how long you stay on but you needed each other and you never raised a question of the disintegration of the coalition. Formally speaking, Dr. Karadzic, you remained in a coalition with the SDA and the HDZ even up to the beginning of the war although you had left the Assembly on the 14th of October, 1991 -- or rather, the deputies of the SDS did. You and I on several occasions had very frank personal discussions. Officially we often had confrontations in respect of my ideas, that is, but as president of the SDS you were also in a position to oppose the even more extremist members of your party because this unfortunate Dr. Zepinic still headed the Ministry of the Interior although he was not obeying the coalition that was in power, if I can put it that way. Also if you wish I can tell you very frankly. There was the example of the conversation you had with the delegation that came from Sokolac and the delegation that came from eastern Herzegovina, the delegation from Banja Luka, and especially I know that you had terrible problems with the chief of the security services centre in Doboj who never agreed with me being on the top, but I did agree that he stay on as chief of the CSB in Doboj because he was the candidate of the SDS. Although at all sorts of meetings with you personally or at the meetings of the parliament of the SDS he asked for a re-examination of my role. So, as I've said, very often we were directly confronted, but also you had to confront even more extremist members of your own party because I headed the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you the following: You remember -- you mentioned that sharp language of mine. Do you ever recall -- actually, can you tell me why I called you and when did we have these unpleasant conversations?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us be perfectly clear. I never thought that these were unpleasant conversations between the two of us. Again I'm saying you were using language that was not appropriate and was not characteristic of the Dr. Karadzic that I knew personally. I have to remind you, Dr. Karadzic - and a few of your ministers in the government of Republika Srpska also said that - you were surrounded by very bad people, people who brought information to you, most often brought you wrong information probably for the following reason: So that you would express the authority of the president of the party, that is probably why you used that kind of language in this aggressive approach in certain characteristic situations. So I cannot say that you personally wanted to offend me or attack me. Quite simply, you were not in a position to give the right answer to the wrong information that had reached you, and very often after this aggressive reaction you would call again and say, Why did this policeman go to Kalesija? Because two men were involved in a brawl. I mean, things that had nothing to do with inter-ethnic relations. But the information that you received was that the policeman was a Muslim, and so on and so forth. Do you understand what I'm saying? Things were similar in other situations too. Zone Boban [phoen] killed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction:

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- hit another football fan at a game and then five years later that man got out and said, I'm a Muslim, not a Serb. So this kind of wrong information that was bandied about -- I'm surprised, you were an experienced man. You're a professional too. Why did you not double-check that information that reached you? You made such a mess in Bosnia-Herzegovina because of minister -- the minister of information [Realtime transcript read in error "misinformation." Velibor Ostojic, the party said that this was an attack against Serbdom and then you talked about the Second World War and you talks about pits and -- this was a terrible, catastrophic situation. Velibor abused that and he was saying at government meetings, Why is Dr. Zepinic concealing information? And I said, Velibor, it is in your interest for us not to reveal the actual results of the investigation. After that neither you nor anyone else from the SDS ever mentioned that again. I'm trying to say that you did not deem it necessary to check the information that receive -- that you received before reacting and you reacted in a way that did not really correspond to the Dr. Karadzic that I knew and the personality of the Dr. Karadzic that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But were you aware of the fact that the SDA, the top leadership of the SDA, was involved in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The translation was not complete. But yes, I'll hear from you first, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I've been struggling since the last few questions before we adjourned yesterday and the questions raised today to identify their relationship with the cross-examination and how they arose out of the cross-examination without success. And the question that is posed now seems to fall squarely within the category of inquiries that are not -- were not raised by the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think the entire cross-examination dealt with issues of Dr. Karadzic's presence at meetings when guns were displayed, his gambling with Arkan, his conduct in wanting to expel people, Muslims, his conduct in wanting to split the MUP, and he has ever right I think at this point to ask Dr. Zepinic whether his conduct and his personality was consistent with the crimes that he's charged with in the indictment: The forcible expulsion of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'll say two things because the latter one I think deals with this comment specifically. First of all, the inquiries made -- raised in cross, as the Court is aware from the specific references to the paragraph -- paragraphs of the statement submitted, were directly responsive to issues raised in the evidence in chief. So it cannot be a circular matter of that type where the Prosecution responds directly to assertions made in the examination-in-chief in a focused manner, and then the redirect seeks to re-open the entire direct examination on the basis that the cross-examination was responsive. So that is not accurate as a broad conceptual matter. But more directly, even taking Mr. Robinson's objection on its face as valid, this question is -- doesn't go to those matters in any event. Now we're looking at not the matter he suggests justifies the inquiries, but instead some issues of broader justification or broader context, all of which was raised by the direct examination and could have been expanded long before the cross-examination responded directly to some of the issues raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I didn't hear in full the question with respect to the SDA. I'm not sure if it's relevant or if you are ready to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you don't mind, just one intervention from me. When I was talking about Velibor Ostojic, translation is saying "the minister of the misinformation." I would -- he was a minister of information not misinformation. I'm sorry for this intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zepinic. It's line 6 of page 6. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, with all due respect, yesterday lines 68, lines 22 and 23, Mr. Tieger suggested, as is his right in cross, to Zepinic that I called him with regard to appointments of Serbian personnel in the MUP. My question is the following: What was the basis or the reasons that I called? I also wanted to ask whether Dr. Zepinic recalls me ever calling him without any reason. I think he said that I called due to certain pressure that was exerted. I wanted to ask the following: Yesterday he confirmed that Hasan Cengic had no right to be involved in the work or meddle with the work of the MUP. Did those people who alarmed me from the field had any reason to be dissatisfied with the influence SDA was exerting over state authorities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the Court may be interested in this and I don't want to pre-empt that. However, I do feel compelled to clarify and rectify an erroneous suggestion by the accused. The only reference I made to the previous conversations was placing in context a question that I then asked about subsequent information that the witness had or didn't have about the division of the MUP, not about the nature of the phone calls, what prompted the phone calls, the broad aspect of those phone calls, which is all dealt with, as I recall, in paragraphs 52 through 72. So, this is an example of the accused using the thinnest thread, that is, a -- any kind of reference whatsoever to a broad topic and then attempting to use that as a hook to re-open a matter that was raised in direct examination that was not explored in cross. Again, the Court may be interested in this for its own reasons, and I'm not trying to be obstructive in that manner, but I've noted over and over again that that's a technique used by the accused and I couldn't let it pass as a justification in this instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow the accused to continue, and if necessary the Chamber will consider whether the Prosecution will have another opportunity to cross-examine if necessary. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic. Did I say the "excuse"? I said the "accused."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I hope you will use the word "excuse" at the end of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 68 there is a quote from Dr. Zepinic's interview to the effect that I called him concerning certain candidates and that Izetbegovic and Kljujic sometimes tried to call him but at the end probably called their own representatives. With the assistance of Dr. Zepinic, I wanted to shed some light on the nature of my interventions. To that end, I'd like to direct your attention to an intercept between -- of a conversation between myself and Dr. Zepinic and it is D364. What can you tell us, Dr. Zepinic, why did I call? What kind of pressure was coming from the field? What kind of pressure was I under that would force me to call you and ask for a clarification?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, as you know, in the coalition partnership you had agreed on a division of certain posts, not only in the Ministry of the Interior but in all other ministries and state bodies and organs to have a restructuring of personnel on the basis of the ethnic key. Given the nature of work and the scope of work I had to deal with at the helm of the Ministry of the Interior, it was our internal arrangement in the ministry to influence directly the top-ranking positions only, such as assistants and deputies to the minister, down to perhaps chiefs of CSBs in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Anything lower than that, the arrangement had been that it would be done by three of my assistants as part of a commission. The commission included Mr. Mandic, Ado Hebib or Mr. Selimovic or Bruno Stojic. Objectively speaking you will understand that I could not physically monitor whether an appointed police station chief who was done appropriately. It's not only you but many others who used to call me about certain work posts and positions which belonged or did not belong to any particular party. To be fair, I was in no position to know what every job entailed in terms of which party had the right to it. That is why you as coalition partners while you were in power before the outbreak of the war, you were never fully able to conduct a restructuring exercise as per national party key, irrespective of the fact that they had their organisational boards. It was Rajko Dukic in the SDS who was tasked with it and the HDZ and the SDA had their own people. I think Boban couldn't deal with it but Kljujic did irrespective of the fact that Boban was the head of the party. However, that task was never completed. It was often intervened, and I would be told: We don't have a commander in this or that municipality. And I didn't eve know whether that commander was supposed to be appointed by the SDS, the SDA, or the HDZ. It was something for my assistants to do and know. Unfortunately, as you could experience in our telephone conversations, there were frequent misuses of position on the part of my deputies, too -- my assistants, actually, and they succumbed to the pressure of certain parties to appoint such people who did not meet the qualifications that were necessarily or who, as people, were not the right people for such jobs but they were only party candidates. If you recall, the HDZ asked for me to be removed because I refused to appoint the head of a police station which was marginal in Bosnia-Herzegovina because he simply lacked appropriate qualifications. And then the HDZ said, Well, Delimustafic was appointed the very same way. And I told Kljujic, Well, this is what you agreed to. If you agreed that that kind of candidate can hold that post, that's fine. But I will not accept to appoint a person like that because the person is not qualified. For example, there was a candidate for the Bihac station who had a criminal file. He had been sentenced for having raped a student in the medical high school. That person should not be a policeman let alone head of station or centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zepinic. So what was my position with regard to personnel being brought to the MUP? Did I ever try to impose anyone who had never been in the MUP and had a criminal file, irrespective of the pressure from the field?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that; however, I can say with certainty as best I can remember with what little intelligence I have left, but I don't remember you ever intervening in favour of someone who had a criminal file for them to be employed in the Ministry of the Interior. But you did, as any other leader, intervene, asking that it should be someone loyal to the party. You did not insist upon and I didn't verify it because it was not my job to do whether such candidates were even members of the party. You were frequently put in a position that you were pressured from the field by the regional or municipal boards to appoint candidates without previous background checks, which created tension between you and me in our telephone conversations and in our private meetings when we discussed such candidates. Let me remind you, Dr. Karadzic, you frequently accepted the arguments that I put to you against certain candidates be appointed to a number of positions. You yourself mentioned the case of Banja Luka. We spent six hours trying to convince each other which would be the right candidate for the position, and my suggestion was adopted in the end. It was a frequent occurrence that there were pressures from the field to appoint personnel who did not meet the qualifications or who had no previous background checks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 3 it was interpreted in the past participle. Dr. Zepinic, I think in the end you did and rather you said that your suggestion was accepted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: We presumed the accused wanted to say it was Dr. Zepinic's suggestion that was adopted. Could the speakers kindly slow down and could Mr. Karadzic kindly repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The gist of it was that I accepted Dr. Zepinic's suggestion not that it was accepted. Doctor, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that against what the local SDS board suggested?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we established yesterday. The regional board of the SDS insisted on a candidate which you had also nominated as the party president. I was against him, not for personal reasons because I didn't know him at all, but I didn't know another candidate who had been at that position prior to your and my arrival. He was in that CSB and based on the information we had it was my estimate that he went about his job professionally which was to be expected in the future. I knew him personally and that was the reason why I insisted on it, and at the end you accepted my proposal that the candidate stay in that position rather than another candidate be placed there who was suggested by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid this is not the document. I'm asking for the 18th of -- 17th of June, D270, it's an intercept where I participate alongside Dr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: To enable Dr. Zepinic to have display, monitor. [Interpretation] We don't need the audio. We need the transcript in both languages. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, please look at the tenth line from the bottom where I ask: "Tell me first did the MUP procure anti-armour weapons?" Do you recall such alarming information even from the army that the MUP was being armed in that way? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I looked at the minutes of the presidential session in 1991 and we submitted a proposal on the restructuring and reequipping of the Ministry of the Interior. Among other things we had envisaged a special Intervention Platoon to be established alongside another special unit which had already been in existence. Both the government and the Presidency approved it, thus approving the procurement of that kind of weapon. The JNA also approved that transport military helicopters be used to procure such anti-armour weapons that would be used by the special platoon. The JNA approved it, otherwise according to the then law it would not be able to procure it. I don't know who it was from the top of the army who told you that we were arming ourselves against the army. Can I read out the conclusions of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps there's no need.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At those sessions of the Presidency of the 15th October and the 16th of December and the 21st and 29th of December as well as at the sessions of the Council for Constitutional Protection, full support was leant to the work and co-operation between the MUP and the JNA in their efforts to preserve peace and security in Bosnia-Herzegovina. At such sessions there were two representatives from the Presidency who were SDS candidates who also agreed with those decisions. We were not arming ourselves against the army. We were not arming ourselves for any other reasons, save, as I have mentioned yesterday, for our security information which indicated that a war is going to -- was going to break out in June 1991. It was being staged. We prolonged it in a way because it was our assessment that in terms of personnel and materiel as well as weapons we needed to be sufficiently well-equipped in order to put a stop to the ensuing war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Serbian page 5, in English page 7, please. Could we have that now. Doctor, please, what you are saying around the middle: "Tomorrow, tomorrow you will be seeing ..."

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that and you don't even have to put a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please read it out nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Hasan Cengic and Osman Brka are to visit me tomorrow." If I may give a free assessment. Perhaps Brka was one of the most extreme members of the SDA and the reason I invited them is the pressure they exerted on Mr. Izetbegovic to appoint persons in the Ministry of the Interior who did not meet the necessary requirements. For example, the chief of the security centre services. That's why I intervened with Mr. Izetbegovic because I was against that. Is it in the interest of the Muslim people to employ criminals in such positions? If that is the case, then let us state this publicly. That's why these two persons were invited to come and see me so that they would be told that they cannot interfere in such a way, to exert pressure on Izetbegovic and then Izetbegovic on me since Cengic was the head of the appointments commission of the SDA and he was supposed to ensure parity on ethnic grounds in the security services and in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that page do you remember the thing I said after that, that: "We haven't appointed a single criminal and we haven't appointed anyone who was never in the MUP before"?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, I already answered that perhaps a minute or two ago. I cannot recall that you personally intervened on behalf of someone who had a criminal record, for such a person to be admitted into the Ministry of the Interior or to be appointed to one of the top positions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So your answer here was: "No, no, no, not a single man of ours. There is nothing that could be said"?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and if you look further on you asked me whether Coric had been replaced. Zoran Coric was an exceptional professional and I said "no." And up to the very end, if I can put it that way, we were under pressure to replace Coric by someone else. Now that you're asking me, believe me, I have no idea what Coric's ethnic background was and I'm not interested at all. I know that he was an electric engineer, that he was a professional, and that he was an adequate person to stay on in that position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we allowed you to continue, but we are struggling to understand how this part arose from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from what Mr. Tieger dealt with on page 68 yesterday, lines 20 to 23, where it was suggested that I called and tried to interfere in the work of the MUP on an unacceptable basis of sorts. But I'll drop the subject now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, regardless of these sharp words on both sides in these official communications, did I show any kind of animosity towards you, or rather, did we keep our mutual respect?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was the case. I don't know what your opinion is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see for yourself that I was intolerant in relation to Muslims or Croats and did I display or have any kind of hatred vis-a-vis them?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that is a question that is very hard to answer, whether you personally hated someone or not, that is your own affair. From the position that I held, I would not want to comment upon that because that's a private matter. I have to point out here that - how do I put this? - that the Serb Democratic Party behaved in a different way until the parliament session was -- until the walk-out from parliament in October 1991. Because after that the policy of the SDS was totally against what your coalition had been based on. As you walked out of the Assembly, according to the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina ceased to exist. It was the duty of the Presidency to dissolve the Assembly and to have early elections. That is what the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina says. That's what the elections law of Bosnia-Herzegovina says. And things went on. If we accept that the European community gave you the mandate and that that was on the basis of the existing laws, then everything that happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina until the 14th of October, 1991, was unlawful against the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and all the legal provisions that had been passed in earlier years. Because you, as the coalition, had not changed any laws. You hadn't changed the constitution. You hadn't adopted any amendments to the constitution. And then you established an unlawful Assembly and you did not have the mandate to do that because you were not elected to create an Assembly of the Serb people and then you established some republic that was not recognised by the Presidency. In all honesty, no one recognised that. This Presidency was unlawful, irregular. So from the point of view of the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina, after the 14th of October, 1991, everything you did was unlawful. When I say "you," I'm not saying "you" personally; I'm referring to your coalition of the three national parties. And you did not break up this coalition even up until the beginning of the war. It was only natural for the speaker of the Assembly to say that the coalition was no longer there after the walk-out of the SDS MPs and that the Assembly could no longer function as a lawful Assembly. And then the Presidency was supposed to call an early election. However, you did not call for an election because you knew on the basis of estimates that you would have lost the election. You can keep shaking your head for as long as you want, Dr. Karadzic, but try to say that I'm wrong when I say that not a single national party then could get 500 citizens at one of their rallies. As presidents you could not even go to another village where you were not in power. You sent me to resolve the question of barricades because you did not dare face the people and say: Remove the barricades. You didn't dare do that. Mr. Izetbegovic didn't dare do that. You were just in an APC, Dr. Karadzic, you and Mr. Izetbegovic. At 3.00 at night we went to the barricades in Sarajevo. Not a single one of you dared to go to the barricades and face the citizens. You asked me to do that. Dr. Zepinic, people respect you, and we are going to do what you -- that they are going to do what you're asking them to do. You needed each other so that you would remain in power. And it is for those reasons that you did not call an election when the Assembly and Presidency, and thereby the government, ceased to exist on a lawful basis.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The pace of speech is too fast for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, I understand your emotions vis-a-vis Yugoslavia and I believe that the late President Tito would have been very happy. However, I'm asking you something else. Did you see a display of intolerance on my part? Did I display hatred vis-a-vis Muslims? Now I'm talking about your knowledge about me.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About you personally, Dr. Karadzic, you know that as the head of the Ministry of the Interior I unfortunately knew everything about all of you and I was supposed to know all of that, how you walked, how you breathed, because I was supposed to protect you because I didn't want any one of you to be in harm's way so that the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina would become even worse than it was. You know full well, Dr. Karadzic, that my ministry kept that dispatch from the Ministry of Croatia that Vojo Seselj not be sent to Croatia. We -- Delimustafic kept that dispatch for three days and then he was -- Seselj was returned to Serbia. However, since he was supposed to be on TV, our assessment was that this would lead to a great deal of tension and that citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina would gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It doesn't say that Seselj had three soldiers only in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Once again, this is too fast for interpretation of each and every word. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please bear in mind that your words have to be translated. Your speed is too high for them to catch up with. I'm not sure you answered the question, but please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, from the position of that knowledge could you see for yourself that I was intolerant towards other ethnic communities and individuals or, for example, that I hated them?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have to remind you that this is your personal affair, whether you hated someone or not. I'm talking about tolerance among parties. Even at the first session on the 20th of October [as interpreted], 1990, during two days you could not even agree on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just for the benefit of the interpreters, it's very obvious when Dr. Karadzic starts to speak as the interpretation from the answer is still being produced, and that can only lead to the problems we -- that the interpreting staff intervened on a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, did you complete your answer to the question that -- whether Mr. Karadzic was intolerant or displayed hatred towards certain people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, before answering your question, I would intervene. I didn't state that it was a session -- first session on 20th of October. It was 20th of December, 1990s. I would appreciate to check this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Doctor, that's one of the problems with going so fast. The interpreters have an immensely difficult job to do and you will appreciate that as someone fluent in both languages. If you leave a pause between the questions and answers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That's better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then please continue. Would you like to continue your answer, Dr. Zepinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can confirm that at sessions of the Assembly there was no agreement whatsoever within the coalition. Now, whether there was any animosity or hatred or enmity on the part of Dr. Karadzic, whether he did not respect Croats or Muslims, that is his personal affair. But for the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina it was catastrophic that this coalition that was supposed to set up a government on the basis of the mandate it had received as a coalition could not even agree on the agenda. Dr. Karadzic, as you know full well, this also contributed to the atmosphere at government sessions, perhaps to a lesser degree, but especially among the members of the Presidency. Your two members of the Presidency decided that they would freeze their work in the Presidency. This institution of freezing does not exist on the basis of the rules of procedure. They did not give up on any one of the perks of office. We did not see any resignations during the work of the coalition that could not agree on anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Zepinic, I'd like us to finish now and I'd like to focus on your knowledge about my behaviour, not my emotions, but the manifestations. You as a -- as the minister of the interior, did you provide policemen for my security detail? Did this security detail include Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and in a way there were some interventions to the effect that this security detail which is given to presidents of political parties on the basis of a decision of the Presidency, this was a special department for protecting persons and buildings. And we were not interested in the ethnic backgrounds of policemen. Policemen were supposed to discharge their duties. I do not recall that you were against anything. I visited you once, if you remember, during a dinner. In front of your building there was a Muslim policeman. You did not object to that because he was carrying out his duties together with his colleague because there were always at least two of them. He was doing his job professionally. You also had some personal body-guards, not only you but the other two leaders as well, and our information said that these persons were not eligible at all. And I personally said that they should not be issued with weapons. And Dr. Koljevic accused me of appointing a security detail that would spy on you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you see any Croats and Muslims among my friends at the time, people I was socialising with?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all had friends and relatives from all ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina, yourself included. I don't think that this is something that this Court should be dealing with, but I can give the names of persons of other ethnic backgrounds that you were friends with. But it wouldn't be right for me to do that. However, in view of the nature of Sarajevo and Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was impossible to have friends in a social circle of only one ethnicity. The people of Sarajevo, Sarajlijas [phoen], had only one ethnicity. They were Sarajlijas, they were people of Sarajevo, and they never raised any ethnic questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about my position vis-a-vis Yugoslavia and Bosnia remaining in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me from my very own position I am going to give you an answer, Dr. Karadzic. There are very few people that I believed loved Yugoslavia and Bosnia more than I did, very few people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was my position about Yugoslavia -- Bosnia remaining in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking privately then we were more or less on the same position. If we're talking about Radovan Karadzic, the president of the SDS, then this is a special atmosphere, if I may put it that way, in which it is not stated precisely what that Yugoslavia would mean. What I meant was Yugoslavia from Zevdjilija [phoen] to Trilav [phoen], not a Yugoslavia that you were a proponent of, some kind of Rump Yugoslavia, Yugoslavia with or without Serbia, greater Croatia, smaller Croatia, a divided Bosnia. Please, Dr. Karadzic, why was there an influence on you just like influence was exerted on the Croatian representative in Bosnia and Herzegovina for Bosnia to have some kind of a subordinate position in the future Yugoslavia in comparison to Serbia and Croatia. Why would Bosnia not have the same equality just like any other republic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you recall, Dr. Zepinic, our historical Serbian-Muslim agreement and was it provided at that time for Mr. Izetbegovic to be the first president?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, allow me to use some statistical indicators --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, please.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was the Belgrade declaration. There was a meeting held by President Milosevic with the Assembly presidents of Serbia, Macedonia, and Bosnia-Herzegovina; and according to that proposal, in view of the Rump Yugoslavia as it was called or as some called it Srboslavia without Croatia and Slovenia, in view of the ethnic composition, it was planned that Muslims would have the prime minister and then this function would rotate. Any future election then would award the position of president to a different ethnic group of that Rump Yugoslavia, which should have been Izetbegovic. However, I must say that in the conversation that Mr. Izetbegovic had with Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Milosevic on the 6th of June in Split, if I can recall, it was clearly stated that the two of them had agreed on the division of Bosnia and Izetbegovic warned that he was not accepting any kind of division of Bosnia. If you remember on the 25th of March, 1991, Tudjman and Milosevic met in Karadjordjevic and agreed that 70 per cent of the BH territory would be given to Serbia and 25 per cent would belong to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 75 per cent later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then in early 1992 they reviewed this and proposed that 65 per cent belonged to Serbia, 20 per cent to Croatia, and 15 per cent to belong to Alija Izetbegovic and the Muslims, that would be along the Bosna River valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Zepinic, neither of us was in that meeting in Karadjordjevic, is that right, and you recall that they never confirmed that conversation?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to dissuade you, Mr. Karadzic. This is something that Tudjman stated publicly, and after the signing of the peace agreement in January 1992 when he said on television that the only solution would be the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina between Croatia and Serbia, about which he and Milosevic had already agreed. They had 48 meetings in Karadjordjevo, Tikves, and Brijoni; then it was Saranic and Smilja Avram [phoen] were entrusted with the drafting of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, all right, Dr. Zepinic. These things are something that we don't know about.

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about them. I'm not just speaking off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's focus on what you know about me. You said today that after the 15th of October, 1991, everything was different. Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber at which point in time at the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina was it that everything was different, there was no more government, Assembly, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an Assembly session on the 10th and 11th of October, 1991, and since it was a very stormy situation and the exchange between you and Mr. Izetbegovic when you said that Bosnia would disappear in two days' time and that 400.000 people in Sarajevo would get killed, and so on and so forth, to which Mr. Izetbegovic replied that he would sacrifice peace for the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Unfortunately, I was sitting, if you can recall, in the first row next to the prime minister and I said, These two are bringing war to us. And Jure Pelivan said, Vito, come on, don't say that and so on. And then you had secret meetings - I'm saying "secret meetings" because this was not disclosed - and my service had this information on Saturday and Sunday to co-ordinate your positions and this was proposed by Mr. Krajisnik. There was no harmonisation of positions among you, so then on the 15th of October, 1991, you demonstratively left the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I mean the deputies of the SDS. And in my estimate, that was the day that was the crucial day for the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If you permit me, I attended a meeting at the Presidency that day with General Kadijevic and his generals who stated at the Presidency meeting -- actually, who just adopted one conclusion, and that is that the Ministry of the Interior should strengthen its co-operation with the Yugoslav People's Army in order to preserve the peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the only conclusion. Dr. Karadzic, by withdrawing the army we had 200.000 from the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina and 65.000 -- 65 per cent of the arms of the former Yugoslavia was concentrated in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is something that should have been controlled. This control could not be executed by disbanding the Assembly and by leaving the Assembly and by having fights among the coalition partners in government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would kindly like us to just deal with what you know about me. What was my position in your view on the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You understood the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the way that Bosnia and Herzegovina could not be an independent state. It had to be a component of Yugoslavia without Croatia and Slovenia, and that that would be Yugoslavia without the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina within it, without independence for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you ever see for yourself that my position was that we would need to expel Muslims and Croats from these areas which would be the Serbian cantons and the Serbian constituent units?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic or President Karadzic, when we're talking about the party, had you in any way directly or through documents said anything like that, I guarantee before this Trial Chamber that you would have been arrested because this was an anti-constitutional decision and you would have violated all the laws in force at the time. So had you at any point mentioned as the president of the party what you have just said you may be assured that you would have been criminally charged without, unfortunately, I have to tell you, any request for immunity to be lifted. Because as president of the party you did not enjoy any form of immunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, this was as far as my position was professionally. As for private contacts you had with me, based on that did you ever get the impression that I was in favour of anybody being expelled from Serbian areas?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot answer that question and I repeat again, had you said something like that to me - I don't know what you meant in view of our profession, Dr. Karadzic, we cannot know what somebody else is thinking - but had you in any way voiced publicly or in writing in a document something like that, you would have been criminally liable. As for you as a person, I have refused many offers to date to write an article about you as a person. So if you would permit me also to do that on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And Cutileiro's Plan that you mentioned or the proposal of the European community of the three -- about the three constituent units, did that imply respect of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How does that arise from Mr. Tieger's cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a question of the rights of ethnic minorities and religious minorities. This was mentioned in the cross-examination. And Dr. Zepinic had his political position, that he was against the secession of the republics, and in particular he disagreed with the idea of the three constituent units. However, he was familiar with Cutileiro's Plan which we accepted and I wanted to ask what this plan was. Did that imply the respect of minority rights?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is a topic you could have raised in your direct examination. I would like you to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Zepinic, for coming to testify. Regardless of our political differences, I'm going to answer your question and, as far as I'm concerned, our mutual respect is intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And perhaps if my transcript is going on, did the SDS party in its programme include the policy of the expulsion of Muslims and what would have happened with that party, again along the lines of what you said would have happened to me?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm talking about documents before the 14th of October, 1991. Had the service had information of that sort at its disposal, we would have definitely initiated the question of whether that party could survive in view of the amendment to the constitution adopted by the Presidency in March of 1990 of that year, meaning six months before your elections, which clearly stated that a party that aims in its programme an exclusively national character could not be registered or could not function. This would include the splitting of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Dr. Zepinic, unless my colleagues have questions for you, then that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you -- but before that, yes, I may have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your statement ends with the sentence that: "We migrated to Australia in February 1993." Could you tell us in a nutshell what you did since then?

utterances.speaker: VITOMIR ZEPINIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1993. You mean since 1993 since arriving in Australia? Well, you know like any immigrant who came to a country that he doesn't know anything about, not knowing English, Your Honour, the first things that I did was some construction work, painting roofs, painting in order to provide for my family because I simply did not wish to accept social assistance because I thought that that would not be a good example for my children. Once I learned a little bit of English, I then applied to have my qualifications recognised. I got a job in a state hospital. I had a job. Then I started a private practice. I have a very successful private practice, psychological clinic. We dealt specifically with PTSD. I can say that I had patients of all ethnicities. I'm talking about patients from the area of the former Yugoslavia. I had patients from Croatia, Serbia, Macedonia, from all parts of our country. And it was a great pleasure to have that happen. Unfortunately, most of my patients knew that many of those who had perpetrated crimes such as rape against them were living in Australia. Because there was no law recognising the crimes committed in the former Yugoslavia before 2003. This is something that I would not want to deal with then for certain. Because of certain writings in the Australian press in which I was declared as a war criminal, among other things, and as being a commander of some sort of special forces with Dr. Karadzic until December 1993. Dr. Karadzic, you failed to pay me for that function. And then already at that time I was paying taxes on the work that I was doing in Australia. So this was a very uncomfortable situation which made my family, in particular my children -- I mean, there were threats that -- there was some bad consequences. I closed the clinic. My family went to London. And then I asked the British government under a programme of highly -- for highly skilled migrants, TA1, because I had a doctorate and other qualifications, my mandate was extended. So I have been in England for the past four years. In the meantime I worked up there as a lecturer at Queen Mary University in London as a senior lecturer in psychiatry. Then I worked privately a little bit. In the meantime, if you're interested, I published two professional books, some articles. I took part in various conferences. And if I may say so, I have continued to work as one of the prominent experts in post-traumatic stress disorders and this is what I'm doing. I'm not easing up in terms of my activities and I intend to contribute as much as I can to the profession. I don't intend or nor am I interested in any kind of political activities. If you're interested, yes, it's true that for the first time I visited my former country two years ago because I was invited to a wedding of my best friend, Fadil Djozo, who is a Muslim. And if you're interested in that as well and Dr. Karadzic knows that very well, when Mico Stanisic arrested me the first thing she said was, We killed Fadil. We killed your Fadil. So that would go to somebody's honour, record of honour. Anyway, I can also say that I know and many asked me if I was afraid for my security in view of what my job was before and then am I afraid for my safety in view of my still unchanged positions for the past two decades. The only thing that I would regret would be if something happened to my family. Unfortunately, something did happen to my mother. But you know, this is something -- I'm not a hero, Your Honour, by far. I did not get any recognition from anyone for what I was doing to secure peace. This is probably the fate of today's time to come out of it the way you come out of it. And let me just say this: I used to say that I ended up in the same way that my country ended up, the country that I loved very much. It had a lot of recognition in the world, everybody loved it and everybody tried to destroy it; this is more or less my fate too. I hope this answer satisfies you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Doctor. That concludes your evidence. Thank you again for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are free to go. We will rise all together. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at seven to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Batinic. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Batinic, before you start giving evidence I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the accused, the Prosecution, or the Judges if you believe your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean that something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for having committed an offence or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you believe that your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Batinic. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Batinic.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you and remind myself to speak slowly and to make sufficient pause between question and answer, so as to have everything interpreted. You can follow the cursor on the screen. Once it's stopped, the interpretation is over. Did you provide a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court 1D7212.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the statement before you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read it and signed it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the last page where the signature is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it accurately reflect what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you today would your answers be basically the same as contained in the statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: The essence would not be changed; that is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to tender this document under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, in addition we're offering two associated exhibits. Two others are admitted and we would ask that they be added to our 65 ter list as we hadn't interviewed in witness at that time that it was submitted. Those two documents are 1D12005 and number 17452.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll grant the request and admit the statement as well as two associated exhibits. Shall we give the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the statement 65 ter 1D7212 will be Exhibit D2930; 65 ter number 1D12005 will be Exhibit D2931; and 65 ter number 7452 will be Exhibit D2932.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to read out a summary of Mr. Tomislav Batinic's statement next in the English language. [In English] Tomislav Batinic was born on 25th of January, 1995 [sic], in the village of Bereg, Rogatica municipality. He finished primary and secondary school in Rogatica, and in 1979 he graduated from the faculty of economics in Sarajevo. He did his compulsory military service in Bela Crkva in the motor vehicle unit. Tomislav Batinic became the vice-president of the Rogatica Municipal Assembly after the multi-party elections. During the war he was president of the Rogatica Municipal Assembly. He does not think that there were any ethnic conflicts in Rogatica until the multi-party system began. During the first half of 1990 the SDA, Muslim party, was founded and the SDS was not founded until -- was not founded until the 3rd of September, 1990, concerning Rogatica municipality. He knew that the Muslims were a majority in BH and they frequently emphasised that BH was theirs. Tomislav Batinic was aware that when the army was mobilised many of the Muslims from Rogatica boycotted the mobilisation and this was similar in other areas. It was clear that the SDA encouraged the Muslims not to respond to the call-up. Those who did respond were returned home a few days later through an SDA-organised operation and Mr. Tomislav Batinic considers this to be the first concrete move to divide the unity of the JNA. This mobilisation was unsuccessful and afterwards the distancing of the Serbs and Muslims became more prominent and inter-ethnic division drastically intensified. The JNA then took action to requisition the conscripts' files from the premises of the Secretariat of National Defence in Rogatica, to gain insight into records of the personnel deployed in the 216th Brigade, and they deployed men fit for service to the Muslim units. Due to these actions, it was not possible to mobilise soldiers in the -- Serb soldiers in the 216th Brigade as the Muslims possessed the only valid record of the military conscripts. With the full engagement of Ramiz Alajbegovic, the police reserve force were mobilised, which included a large number of Muslims. All the reserve forces were provided with weapons and these activities caused apprehension among the Serbs who felt endangered. Faced with these dangers, the Serbs began organising gradually. Night guards were established in Serb settlements, and the Territorial Defence was formed to protect the Serbian people. In an attempt to overcome problems and settle daily life issues, the Serbian Assembly was created with a Serbian president; however, this never actually took place due to the ever-changing landscape. The legislative and executive authorities functioned but with great difficulties. Tomislav Batinic considers that the media contributed to the situation by creating an atmosphere of fear and anxiety. Muslims set up barricades in the front of buildings and strictly controlled who entered and left the buildings. It was realised that the best solution to avoid an armed conflict was to divide the municipality into Serbian and Muslim parts. This idea was discussed at a Crisis Staff session -- sessions and the Executive Committee, and the police were convinced that this way -- this was the only way to preserve peace. The decision was formally declared on the 2nd of May, 1992, although this was postponed because the Serbian side thought that an agreement could be reached. It was soon realised that the decision was a reality. Tomislav Batinic considers it unlikely that the JNA armed the Serbs in Rogatica without his knowledge. The Crisis Staff was formed a month before the division of the municipality. The staff worked on finding ways to overcome the problems, protecting the population, housing refugees, and other such tasks. The Crisis Staff never adopted the position or rendered the decision on the forcible removal of the Muslim population, nor did it incite the other institutions to do so. When the division -- divisions occurred, the Muslim police remained where they were and the Serbian police moved out into another area. After these events Serbs began leaving town en masse and found accommodation with their relatives on the outskirts of the city. Chaos reigned in the town and many of the organs of the Serbian municipality had to relocate and Muslims were erecting barricades in the town. Tomislav Batinic considers that when the Muslims killed Drazenko Mihajlovic in May the 22nd, 1992, or around, the war definitely started in Rogatica municipality. Those Muslims from the town who surrendered their arms moved from the centre of town to the secondary school building and were housed there temporarily with Serbian and Croatian families. At the end of July 1992 the town was liberated from Muslim extremists and on their retreat they torched the transformer station, meaning Rogatica didn't have electricity for five months. Tomislav Batinic denies that the Crisis Staff or any other organ reached the decision to turn the secondary school building in Rogatica into a holding centre. Tomislav Batinic visited the secondary school centre and spoke to many of the families. He also assisted with some to travel and find accommodation. The Executive Committee was formed after the Serbs returned to the town and the Crisis Staff was disbanded. There were numerous problems to deal with including inventories for abandoned apartments, accommodation of refugees, and ensuring that hospital, schools, and companies were functioning and serving the population. The Executive Committee adopted decision to ensure that all living conditions were guaranteed for all villages including Muslim villages who expressed loyalty to the Serbian authorities. Tomislav Batinic endeavoured to ensure peace and safety in the Muslim villages who expressed loyalty to them and he visited the villages in person. On the 30th of November, 1992, he travelled to Burati, Muslim village, to deliver aid, but the vehicle ran over an anti-tank mine and he was seriously wounded. He was aware of paramilitary organisations who would lie and wait to loot houses, and on one occasion they attempted to remove a Muslim from the school centre. He was not aware the reason for the detention of the people in Rasadnik, but when the Executive Committee asked they received the response that it was mainly Serbians who were detained and the largest number of the people detained were Serbs and no verbal or physical mistreatment of detainees occurred. Tomislav Batinic categorically states that the Serbian representatives either in the joint or in a -- the separate organs of authority, never contributed anything to cause a conflict or create intolerance and especially not to forcibly remove the Muslims from Rogatica or other settlements in which they were in the majority and to surrender authority to the Serbs in the entire territory of the municipality. [Interpretation] This concludes the summary. At this point I have no questions for Mr. Batinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Batinic, as you have noted your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. Katrina Gustafson. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Batinic.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to start with a straightforward question. This is not in your statement anywhere, but if you could just confirm that you were an SDS member; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 14 of your statement you describe the formation of the Serbian Municipal Assembly in Rogatica and you say that it was formed at the end of 1991. And that Assembly was formed in accordance with SDS Main Board instructions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: It is correct that the Serbian municipality was established in late December 1991. Unfortunately, at that time I had not received any instructions of the Main Board of the SDS. I was not present at their meetings because I was not a member of the Main Board of the SDS. It was our belief that it comprised prominent Serb citizens who enjoyed a certain degree of authority in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to P3407.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 17 the witness stated that it was established because of their belief that things were supposed to be that way and that it was to comprise prominent citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, this is a report on the activities of the Rogatica municipal organs compiled by Milorad Sokolovic and dates from 1993. If we could go to page 5 of the English and page 4 in the B/C/S. And under Roman numeral II, halfway through the second paragraph -- or, sorry, the first sentence of that paragraph refers to the creation of the Serb Municipal Assembly at the end of December 1991, just as you stated in your evidence. And the second sentence says: "Serb Municipal Assembly included also, as per instructions of the main Serb Democratic Party Board, SDS Local Board Presidents from the area of the municipality ..." And the Chamber has received evidence of SDS Main Board instructions issued at around the same time that precisely required the inclusion of SDS local board presidents for municipalities like Rogatica where Serbs were a minority. And I refer to P5, instruction 4, of Variant B. Now, whether you were aware of it at the time or not, this passage reflects the fact that the Serb Municipal Assembly in Rogatica was formed pursuant to SDS Main Board instructions; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: In any case, I read that document two or three days ago. I didn't know of it before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So two or three days ago you did, in fact, realise that the Serb Municipal Assembly was created pursuant to SDS Main Board instructions; do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And also at paragraph 14 of your witness statement you said that the Serbian municipality -- sorry, the Serbian Municipal Assembly never started functioning and it all remained solely on paper. And then at paragraph 19 you indicate that you were elected president of the Serbian municipality of Rogatica only upon the division of the municipality in early May. So just so I understand your position, is your position that the Serb Municipal Assembly did not start functioning until the municipality was formally divided on the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Let me explain this. As far as I recall, as of the 24th of December, the Serb Assembly was established in Rogatica municipality comprising those representatives we mentioned before. It was nominal only because the situation in the field changed from one day to the next. The citizens asked for us to do so because there was a lot of anxiety and fear in town. We established the Rogatica Municipal Assembly, but that's what we left it at until further notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So is it your position that it never held any -- that there were no Serb Municipal Assembly sessions until the 3rd of May?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: No. My associates and I believed that there would be an agreement reached at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina and we were simply trying to buy ourselves more time by making decisions like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. That's not quite an answer to my question. My question was what your -- whether there were any Serb Municipal Assembly sessions between the time it was created, in late December 1991, and the time the municipality was formally divided on the 3rd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to put to you that's not true and the Serb Municipal Assembly began functioning immediately by holding its inaugural session on the 26th of December, 1991, at which you were elected Assembly president. Do you agree or disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I guess it could have been the Variant B or the second level, when the Assembly sessions were organised in order to have the authorities put in place, when the Executive Board was established as well. That's probably it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 8 of this document in English and page 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Batinic, you can see at the top of the English and about a third of the way down in the B/C/S there is a paragraph that says: "On inaugural session of the Municipal Assembly held on 26 December 1991 Tomislav Batinic was elected President of the Municipal Assembly, while Deputy President is not yet elected." Does that remind you of the fact that an inaugural session of the Serb Municipal Assembly was elected almost immediately upon its formation and you became its president?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to P2835, page 3 in the English and also page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a report on the work of the Crisis Staff between April and June 1992 and you are familiar with this document because it's referenced in your statement. And if we go to the bottom paragraph in both languages it says: "When it is said that the Crisis Staff adopted 18 decisions under its jurisdiction, it is necessary to remember that the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Rogatica at its session on 15 April 1992 by special ruling authorised the Crisis Staff to perform the duties of the Executive Committee ..." et cetera, et cetera. This is another reflection of the fact that the Serb Municipal Assembly was in fact functioning and holding sessions prior to the 3rd of May, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: It is certain, given the fact that the Assembly was constituted only, its speaker was elected, whereas the Executive Board or any of its organs were not appointed nor were any executive bodies. The Assembly authorised the Crisis Staff to act as the Executive Board until it is being -- until it is constituted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But you don't deny that contrary to what you said a few moments ago that the Serb Municipal Assembly was, indeed, functioning and holding sessions prior to the 3rd of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: It sat twice. For example, at the second session it tasked the Crisis Staff to carry out the functions of the executive organ of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 18 of your statement you said that a Serb Crisis Staff was formed a month before the division of the municipality, and so that would be early April 1992. You don't mention this in your statement, but you were a Crisis Staff member; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, by virtue of my other position which was the deputy speaker of the Assembly. At the time I was deputy speaker of the joint Assembly of Rogatica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right. This was a Serb Crisis Staff, right, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Again I'm going to put to you that the Serb Crisis Staff was actually formed before early April and it was only expanded in early April on -- precisely on the 8th of April, but there was a Crisis Staff in existence before that time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be more precise. Is it the Crisis Staff as an organ of the authorities or of the party, so as not to have any confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that can be clarified in your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 1 of this document in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, as the report indicates, the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality was established at the session of the Main Board of the SDS, I assume that's of Rogatica, of 8th April 1992. And then in the next paragraph it says: "The former Crisis Staff was extended at the session and since 8 April 1992 ... it consisted of ..." And then it lists a number of people, including you. Now, that reference to extending the Crisis Staff at the 8 April session is a reflection of the fact that there was a Crisis Staff in existence before the 8th of April, and on the 8th of April it was expanded and became the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And is it right that you were a member of both the earlier Crisis Staff and remained a member of the expanded Crisis Staff until it ceased functioning in the summer of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Certainly. If I may just explain briefly. The previous Crisis Staff faced a crisis, and after the resignation of the president of the former Crisis Staff and two of us who were members, a new Crisis Staff was elected on the 8th of April, 1992. I was re-elected into the new Crisis Staff as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you resigned from the earlier Crisis Staff at some point. When was that, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it may have been, say, the month of March.
