We talked to the Crisis Staff and the work group of the Muslims in relation to the division of the municipality in order to keep the population. We talked and we came to the conclusion that at that point in time before the situation was resolved at the level of the entire state, it would be best if we passed a resolution on the division of the municipality. However, then the TO was established within the Serb people, and they asked us to do that quickly. We did not agree to that because the division is a major process and we said that it required time. They wanted us to do it as fast as possible and then we tendered our resignations if somebody could do it better.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, your specific concern and conflict with the Serb TO in March was due to the fact that that TO, led by SDS Main Board member Rajko Kusic, was ruthlessly rushing with threats to attack the town unless the municipality and the police station were immediately divided; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, of course our views differed on that because we were in favour of agreement, discussions, and I think that everything led to that. However, there were people who thought along different lines, you see, and they thought that this could be done and over with within two hours. That's not what we thought. We said at one point in time, if there's somebody who can do this better, let them go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay could we go to P6105, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, this is a letter that you, along with Mr. Veselinovic and Mr. Ujic, signed and sent to Dr. Karadzic on the 25th of March, 1992. And it states that the Crisis Staff is not able to carry out its decisions due to a group of armed Serbs headed by a member of the Main Board, Rajko Kusic, who was ruthlessly rushing with threats to attack the town in case the municipality and the public security station are not unconditionally divided. You say that the Crisis Staff, in compliance with your, presumably Dr. Karadzic's instructions, believes that the factual division on the ground should be and is already there, but you state that the official division must be accompanied by laws issued by Serbian ministries as well as party agreements on the highest level. And then you state: "We believe it is dangerous to be the originator of the war situation when the Serbian people are not sufficiently prepared and provided." Now, it's clear from that last sentence that one of your concerns with what Rajko Kusic was doing at the time was that the Serbian people were not sufficiently prepared at that point for war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: It is correct, but let me just explain this. In that period of time there was mobilisation of personnel into the 216th Brigade that was at Han Pijesak. All able-bodied Serbs basically responded to the call-up and it was only able-bodied Muslims who stayed on in town. They boycotted the mobilisation of the JNA. Since the police station had the weapons that were distributed to the reserve police force, mainly Bosniaks, Muslims, Serbs did not respond to the mobilisation of the police station, and then there was fear, hopelessness, and a lack of safety in town. The people expected the establishment of that kind of Territorial Defence unit from among the able-bodied Serbs who had stayed on in town. This happened in Borike and a small unit of the Territorial Defence was established; it was headed by Mr. Kusic. They were concerned because all the able-bodied Serbs were outside Rogatica. They feared for the safety of their families and this probably affected the command of the Territorial Defence, and they probably thought that this division could be carried out very quickly. However, we thought that a different path should be followed because we were already involved in discussions with the Bosniak side. And to be quite honest, I did not think that we would succeed in this division. But I thought that we could buy some time, counting on certain agreements to be reached at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We did not want to give up on discussions, agreements, accommodation of views, but that is why we tendered our resignations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You wrote to Dr. Karadzic personally and informed him of the situation and the conflict you were having with Rajko Kusic and it's common ground I think that Rajko Kusic did not, in fact, attack Rogatica town until the 22nd of May, approximately two months after this. So did Dr. Karadzic or somebody else on the republic level intervene to resolve this conflict you were having with the Serb TO?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what? We had very poor communication at the time with the then-president, Dr. Karadzic. Perhaps I remember that once I had the opportunity of being at Dr. Karadzic's and he just told me: Try to endure, just negotiate, negotiate, negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But you don't -- you're not aware of the extent or nature of Dr. Karadzic's contacts with Rajko Kusic, an SDS Main Board member, are you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And one last question on this document. You were stating that you were going to resign from all your positions in the SDS and the municipality and put yourselves at the disposal of the JNA. If I understand correctly, you did resign from the then-existing Crisis Staff, but then became a member of the Crisis Staff -- expanded Crisis Staff on the 8th of April. You did not resign from your position as Municipal Assembly president and you did not join the JNA. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully. Well, I wouldn't want you to misunderstand what I'm saying, but at that point in time I was a person who enjoyed a great deal of authority among the people, the citizens. I held certain political positions beforehand. I held various offices as president of the youth organisation in Rogatica, president of the socialist alliance of the working people in Rogatica. And at that point they did not allow me to retreat. Probably they trusted me as a person.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move on to something else now. At paragraph 23 of your statement you state that in May 1992 the Muslims killed a Serb by the name of Drazenko Mihajlovic, and you claim that this is considered the start of the war in Rogatica. The Chamber has received evidence including from Defence witness Mile Ujic who was the Chief of Staff of the Rogatica Brigade in 1992, that on the 22nd of May the Rogatica Brigade launched a shelling and infantry attack on Rogatica town and Muslim villages in the municipality. You don't deny that that attack took place, do you? For the record, the transcript pages 33459 to 33460, where Mr. Ujic's evidence.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Before that, certainly people were leaving town, people of both ethnic backgrounds. The organs of both municipalities had relocated. Quite simply, the town was no man's land. Only those who saw some interest of their own remained in town. They were involved in looting, they were shooting, and they were barricades all over in town and outside. For security reasons we withdrew from town and I never entered town until the conditions were right to enter town. It is a fact that sometime in May 1992 this young man got killed, and then definitely there was this close contact between both armed forces and we believed that that day was a turning point in terms of the beginning of the war in the territory of Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I take it that you do not deny that that attack took place on the 22nd of May, as I described it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that then about 12 persons lost their lives, persons of Serb ethnicity. On that day, yes, an attack did take place, an attack against Rogatica and the forces clashed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And the Chamber has received evidence in the form of General Mladic's military notebooks that five days prior to this 22nd of May attack, so on the 17th of May, representatives of Rogatica municipality attended a meeting in Sokolac, also attended by General Mladic, Dr. Karadzic, and Mr. Krajisnik. And at that meeting

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC SAID
utterances.text: "We are looking for results from the army. That's their job." And that's P1477, pages 349 to 352. Were you at that meeting, Mr. Batinic; and if not, do you know who from Rogatica attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I can say that I was not there for sure, but it must have been someone who was in charge of the Territorial Defence then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Would it have been logical for Rajko Kusic to be in attendance at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So is it fair that you don't know what was said or decided at that meeting regarding the army's tasks in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't know, that's for sure. I state that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Batinic, the -- I'm going to put to you that the killing of Drazenko Mihajlovic was, at most, an excuse for the Bosnian Serbs to launch the attack on Rogatica on the 22nd of May. The -- I'll also put it to you that the truth is that the Bosnian Serb forces in Rogatica led by Rajko Kusic, VRS brigade commander and SDS Main Board member, attacked and took over Rogatica because of Rogatica's strategic importance in the eyes of the Bosnian Serb leadership. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, I'm not an officer and I don't know about these military virtues or strategic objectives that the army and certain state organs had. I certainly cannot give an answer in the affirmative because I was not involved and basically I wasn't in charge either.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. The Chamber has also received evidence that at the 53rd Assembly Session, Republika Srpska Assembly Session, on the 28th of August, 1995, a time when I believe you had, in fact, become a member of that Assembly, that Dr. Karadzic said - and this is at P988, page 68: "To tell the truth, there are towns that we grabbed for ourselves and there were only 30 per cent of us. I can name as many of those as you want, but we cannot give up the towns where we made up 70 per cent. Don't let this get around, but remember how many of us there were in Bratunac, how many in Srebrenica, how many in Visegrad, how many in Rogatica, how many in Vlasenica, Zvornik, et cetera. Due to strategic importance they had to become ours and no one is practically questioning it anymore." Were you present at the Assembly when Dr. Karadzic said this; and if not, did you hear about these words?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Firstly, in that period I was not president of the municipality of Rogatica after May 1995. I don't remember the date when I was co-opted as an MP in the Assembly of Republika Srpska because I was on the list of MPs who did not win a sufficient number of votes to become members of the Assembly, but then I was co-opted because there were some MPs who returned their mandate. I don't remember whether I was at the Assembly at the time or co-opted, but I did not hear about this statement of Mr. Karadzic's later on either, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like to move on now to what you said about the Rogatica secondary school, which at paragraph 26 you describe as a location where families from Rogatica were accommodated, and you state that you told some of the families there that they were free to return to their homes in the town. You don't say anything in your statement about how these people came to be accommodated at the secondary school, but it's true, is it not, that a great many of them had been taken there by the Rogatica Brigade after they had been captured in their villages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, Madam Prosecutor, at one point in time I said that all of Rogatica was practically a war zone. We moved into the outskirts of town. The town itself was basically no man's land. We don't know what happened in town and in the territory of the municipality of Rogatica. There was thunder all over. They were exchanging accusations that the other side was shelling Rogatica, attacking it. We did not enter town until it could be entered. I know and there were conflicts in town, I was away on official business then in Belgrade. When I returned I heard that there had been contact between the units and that civilians, citizens, of military age came to the school, the secondary school. That's what we heard. There were civilians, military-age men, et cetera, at the secondary school. I heard that certain persons were saying that all of those who are not able-bodied should move to this collection centre at the secondary school in Rogatica. We did not go there then because it was all risky. And when the citizens relocated to the secondary school we heard that they were being secured by the military police and civilian police. At any rate, the information we had was that they were provided with food there, that it was safe for them there, that nothing bad was happening down there and so on. Quite simply, that's what we heard -- what I personally heard from persons who were in charge of the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So it's your position that you never heard from the brigade command that they were taking civilians from villages to the Rogatica secondary school; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did you ever hear from the brigade command that they were taking civilians from villages to the Rogatica secondary school, Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: No, no. I never did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 24599, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I note, for the record, that this document has actually been MFI'd as D2913, but as there is no translation yet we've uploaded the document both English and B/C/S here. And when I'm finished with it we can certainly add the English to the existing exhibit. And this is a letter that you wrote to the Rogatica Brigade command and the gist of it is at the at the bottom where you say: "We invite you to immediately inform us in writing about whether there are prisons and collection centres on the territory of the municipality of Rogatica so that we could in turn inform the Presidency about it in writing." And this is a letter you wrote on the 25th of November, 1992. And if we could now go to Exhibit D2914. This is Rajko Kusic's response to you. You can see in the subject it references your -- the previous document by number and date and it says: "Since the first day of combat activities, the members of Rogatica Brigade have treated civilian population according to the Geneva Conventions. We have separated civilian population from extreme combatants we have fought against. With your approval, we have gathered civilians at the secondary school, church centre, and DP 'Ergela' in Rogatica. In accordance with circumstances, we were providing them with the same food our soldiers on the line had three times a day. "After sufficient number of civilian population was gathered, you have organised their transport to Sarajevo, Bijeljina, Olovo, Zepa, which was escorted by civilian police." So, Mr. Batinic, contrary to what you said a few moments ago, the brigade command did inform you directly that they were taking civilians to the Rogatica secondary school; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, you certainly reminded me. I sent a letter like this to the police station -- I don't know what day it was - to take care of people, property, private property, state property. And as far as I can see, we wrote to the command of the Rogatica Brigade here as well and we warned them too. I certainly do not accept the allegation that we organised the collection centres and that we secured them. The civilian authorities, the Crisis Staff, none of us ever wrote or ordered them or asked them for that. We could not do that because we were in a completely different part of the municipality. And we asked them to act in accordance with all of these international conventions and not to hold people in areas where they shouldn't be.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Batinic, the Chamber has heard a number of witnesses say that, in fact, they were taken to the secondary school by soldiers, imprisoned there, and then many of them were expelled to the locations listed in this report from Rajko Kusic. So, for example, Elver Pasic gave evidence that on the 7th of June Serb soldiers arrested him together with other Muslims who were hiding in the cellar of a building in Rogatica, seeking shelter from the shelling. Pasic was taken with his mother and grandmother to the secondary school, where he was detained until 27 June when he was taken away and eventually detained at Batkovic prison in Bijeljina. Armin Bazdar testified that on the 4th of August, 1992, Serb soldiers took him and his family from their home in Seljani village to Rogatica high school. About 90 Muslims from his village were detained there along with many more Muslims who had been detained there prior to his arrival. The next day military-aged men were separated from the women and children. The women and children were loaded into buses and trucks like cattle and then taken to Hresa where they were later exchanged. The men were taken to Rasadnik and detained. Sefik Hurko testified that Rajko Kusic took him, his father, his mother to Rogatica secondary school where they were imprisoned with other Muslim men, women and children. And Alija Isakovic gave evidence that he was captured in Rogatica town and detained at the high school from 10 June 1992 to the 5th of August, 1992, again the women and men were separated. The women were taken to Sarajevo for exchange while the men were taken to Rasadnik. Mr. Batinic, that is the reality of what was happening to the Muslims at the Rogatica secondary school, is it not?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I can neither confirm nor deny. If the witnesses stated that they were in the high school building, I do not deny it. However, it was not under our authority. What happened there was within the authority of the brigade command in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I would like to move on put perhaps 65 ter 24599, the English could be attached to Exhibit D2913 and we have no objection to its full admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We have basis now to admit the MFI D2913 in full. We'll do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Batinic, at paragraph 35 you state categorically that the Serbian organs of authority never contributed anything to forcibly remove the Muslims from Rogatica and you claim that their organs of authority and the SDA reached the decisions on moving out on their own. Mr. Batinic, the Muslims of Rogatica did not leave the municipality because of any SDA decision to that effect. They left because their homes and villages were being shelled and they were being massacred and abused by the Bosnian Serb forces, principally the Rogatica Brigade led by Rajko Kusic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: For the most part, the area of Rogatica and town itself was abandoned by both Serbs and Muslims. At some point in time, Rogatica as a whole was a war zone. In any case, the Serbs mainly withdrew to the north and Muslims to the southern part of town towards Gorazde. I believe that neither of the sides had it easy. As for what was taking place in the town itself, we had no influence there because we had no access to the town. We couldn't influence any activities or work of the brigade and its people or of any other units such as paramilitary units, be it Muslim or Serbian. The authority was in the hands of the VRS and the brigade had its own system of command and the issuing of orders.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, you haven't precisely answered my question. I'd like to go to P1001. Now, this is a warning from General Sipcic, SRK corps commander, to Rajko Kusic personally. And it says: "Kusic, I strictly forbid you to take any action on your own unless I personally approve, particularly any form of mopping up of anybody's villages. "For the last time," double underlined, "I am warning you to refrain from massacre, rampaging, abusing the innocent population of any nationality." And consistent with the contents of this document, the Chamber has received evidence of convictions by the Bosnian state court in recent years of Rogatica Brigade members for crimes against Muslims in the town and villages of Rogatica. I refer to P6106, the 2007 conviction of Radislav Ljubinac for forcible transfer of Muslims to and away from Rogatica secondary school and beating prisoners at Rasadnik. P6107, the 2006 conviction of Dragoje Paunovic aka Spiro for the execution of prisoners taken away from Rasadnik. Mile Ujic confirmed his position as a Rogatica Brigade unit commander at transcript 33471 and D1665, that's the 2009 conviction of Stojan Perkovic for murder, cruel treatment, unlawful detention and rape committed against Muslims from a number of different villages. And Perkovic's position as a unit commander in the brigade is identified in P2832, page 4. Now, Mr. Batinic, the contents of General Sipcic's warning and these recent convictions reflect the terror that the Rogatica Brigade was inflicting on the Muslim population of Rogatica, don't they?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: This order, this document produced by Mr. Sipcic to Kusic, is something I see for the first time. They had their own line of reporting, command, and ordering. I have nothing to add. Probably Mr. Sipcic had information we did not have in detail. Once again I reiterate that we were busy with organising civilian life and the functioning of companies, educational institutions, health institutions, and other aspects of life in the municipality. As regards the brigade, its commander had enormous authority and he wouldn't allow anyone interfere with the affairs of the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. On that note I'd like to go to 65 ter 17452 which now has a Defence exhibit number. It was an associated exhibit. I don't recall it at the moment. This is the message, Mr. Batinic, that you discuss at paragraph 27 of your statement that Dr. Karadzic sent to you and other municipalities on the 14th of July, 1992, in which he states that: Municipality presidents must bear the responsibility to ensure the protection of Croats and Muslims who hand over their weapons and do not intend to fight. Now, you made it very clear in your answer to some of my previous questions that you had no influence on the work or activities of the brigade and its members and that the VRS had its own system of command that you were not a part of. And in relation to that system of command, the Chamber has received evidence of that military chain of command rewarding and commending the Rogatica Brigade and its commander Rajko Kusic. I refer to P6108, that's General Galic's December 1992 congratulations to the Rogatica Brigade for its successes in 1992. P5586 which is Dr. Karadzic's personal promotion of Rajko Kusic to the rank of captain first class. And P2832, reflecting the fact that the entire brigade received the order of Nemanjic. Kusic was given the order of Milos Obilic and Stojan Perkovic who was mentioned was convicted in 2009 for crimes against Muslims was singled out for commanding one of the best units in the brigade. Now, in this context, Mr. Batinic, it was a disingenuous gesture for Mr. Karadzic to assert in his telegram that the municipality president was responsible for protecting the non-Serb population in Rogatica while he himself commanded a military structure that promoted and rewarded those who were committing crimes against that population. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of these commendations. I hear of it for the first time. As regards Dr. Radovan Karadzic's document, as the president of Rogatica Municipal Assembly I tried to protect all those villages inhabited by Muslims of which there were five or six: Satorovici, Osovo, Okruglo, Tmorni Do, Burati and perhaps another one. I went there personally providing them with food and health care. I frequented those villages, given the fact that it was easier on those people when I appeared because they believed me. That's why I visited them frequently. As for this document, it was probably sent then and I see it now. I do not deny its being sent. I can't discuss its content and who commended who, but I do know for sure that we were in no position to propose or commend and give awards to anyone as civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You just said in your answer that you tried to protect all those villages inhabited by Muslims of which there were five or six. And I take it from that that at a certain point of time there were just five or six villages left in the Serb-held parts of Rogatica where any Muslim inhabitants remained living; is that correct? And if so, at what point of time were there these five or six villages -- sorry, at what point in time had all the Muslims left the other villages aside from these five or six?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Those were the villages one could access. They were not in the war zone. All of the other Serb and Muslim villages were inside the war zone. They were in a difficult position and that's where there was combat. Simply, people moved away wherever they could at any given point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraphs 29 and 30 you refer to the existence of Muslims remaining in some of these villages, you refer to as loyal Muslims. And you say -- you refer specifically to Burati which -- is that the same village as Burati?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Burati, B-u -r-a-t-i.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you say that: "We kept the people in Burati alive and well throughout the entire war." And what about Satorovici, is it your position that they, the Muslims of Satorovici, also remained there throughout the entire war in their village?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, Satorovici, Osovo, Tmorni Do and Okruglo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you said you visited these villages. Did you know an elderly woman by the name of Fatima Potorkevic from Burati?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I did visit a house then where we drank coffee and had lunch. We were hosted by someone who was called Katica, I believe, and there was an infirm grandfather in -- who was bedridden. I don't recall a woman, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. What about a man by the name of Sejdalija Mirvic from Satorovici?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Sejdalija Mirvic, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you know him to be from Satorovici village?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Batinic, I'm going to put it to you that it's not true that the Muslims in these villages remained throughout the entire war, that, in fact, the Bosnian Serb authorities expelled the last remaining Muslims from Rogatica municipality in October 1994. Would you like to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Certainly, but at their request, the citizens requested it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to go to P4867.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you're coming to a close?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have about five minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a prisoner exchange report compiled by the Federation Exchange Commission dated the 15th of October, 1994. And if we go to page 2 of the English and stay on page 1 of the B/C/S, it describes what happened during this exchange and it says at the bottom of the B/C/S/at the top of the English: "The aggressor took advantage of the exchange to expel 87 Bosniaks, Muslims from the villages of Satorovici, Burati, Osovo, Knezina, Kramer Selo, Kozica, Okruglo, Kovanj." And if we go to page 4 in both languages, the middle of the English and the top of the B/C/S it says that: "... Karadzic's Serbs have taken advantage of the 1st October 1994 Agreement ..." And the next sentence says: "In that sense, prior to the exchange Karadzic's Serbs had on 5 October expelled the remaining Bosniak population from four Rogatica villages: 66 women, children, and elderly in total. On the 10th of October they expelled another 21 residents of the villages of Burati and Kovanj, leaving these territories purely Serb inhabited." And if we could go to 65 ter 24462. Sorry, my mistake. 65 ter 24464. This is a "New York Times" article from the same time as the report we just saw and it's in English so I'll just read the relevant parts to you. It's dated the 6th of October, 1994, and it's titled: "Expelled from villages, bewildered Muslims trudge to Sarajevo. "The central image of the Bosnian war was repeated yet again in Sarajevo today when Muslim men, women and children expelled by Serbs from Eastern Bosnia trudged across a city bridge clutching their only remaining possessions in a few ragged sacks. "Dazed and frightened, some of them in tears, they came slowly across the so-called bridge of brotherhood and unity between the Serb-held Grbavica section of Sarajevo and government-held territory. Then as United Nations officials looked on they were bundle onto city buses and taken off to one of the many refugee centres in the Bosnian capital." Then there's a quote: "'Serbian soldiers came to my house today and said I was to leave at once,' said Fatima Potorkevic, aged 75 from the village of Burati near Rogatica in Serb-held Eastern Bosnia. 'I have no idea where I am going.' "Sejdalija Mirvic said his village of Satorovici near Rogatica was entirely emptied of its remaining Muslims today. The Serbian authorities came to each Muslim household and told the families to prepare to leave. They were bundled onto buses to Sarajevo. "'I had these apartments in my house and a small farm with cattle,' Mr. Mirvic, 56, said, 'Now all I have left is in these bags.' He pointed to two bundles on the floor of the bus." Now, Mr. Batinic, you agreed that the Muslims in these villages did in fact leave, although you said it was voluntary, and you said you knew Mr. Sejdalija Mirvic from Satorovici. You don't deny that Mr. Mirvic and Ms. Potorkevic were explaining the truth about what happened to them in their villages, do you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: It is certain that I knew what the situation was in all of the villages and that is why I tried to make the utmost to make their lives easier. I did everything I could to keep them there. I knew that in Burati village Mustafa Prkos came to me and asked me to do everything so that they could move to Sarajevo. I wasn't happy about it, but I mustered my strength and said, Well, Mustafa, if that is your wish, there is no problem. But do not portray that as if we were consciously moving those people out. And I also told him, All this would be for nothing if we died. If we survive we can discuss it because human lives are the most important. I am sorry for all of the heads of families and citizens in general who had to leave their property behind or lost their lives. At the moment in time and the situation we were in, I don't think more could have been done. Now, whether we chose the best course and whether we were sufficiently prepared at the time, there were probably mistakes and failures, but it is certain that I did my utmost to protect those people in Rogatica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So when Ms. Potorkevic said: "'Serbian soldiers came to my house today and said I was to leave at once ...'" Is that something you know about, did you know that the Rogatica Brigade or at that point the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade was doing in those villages at this time?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't know. That is certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you said that people came to you and said to do everything that you could -- and asked you to do everything so that they could move to Sarajevo. Mr. Batinic, the situation in these --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The situation in these people's villages, the security situation, must have been dire for these people to ask you to take them away from their homes, their farms, their livelihoods, places they'd lived all their lives. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I accept that those people, despite the level of protection we could offer, still lived in fear daily, fearing that a stray drunken soldier civilian may come in to mistreat them. Of course we couldn't keep everything under control at all times and certainly those individuals thought along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Batinic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll hear that after the break. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 15 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.26 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This is in response to your inquiry yesterday concerning the request for leave in connection with the second motion for subpoena. I indicated we'd be getting back to you, and as you're aware we tried to respond to the Legal Officer in advance but there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Batinic, today you were asked about your resignation and some misunderstandings or differences between the civilian authorities and the TO, which is something that you discuss in paragraph 16 of your statement. In the second part of the paragraph you say: "The civilian authorities in Rogatica which was hoping for a political solution and believed in the negotiations ..." et cetera, et cetera "is opposed to the TO." Can you tell the Chamber what kind of information did the civilian authorities have that they founded their hopes on and what information did the TO have?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, we expected that a political solution would be possible and we acted in that vein. We did what we could. However, I suppose that the TO received other information along other lines which was against a dialogue, but rather that different means be applied. It was our belief that we should engage in negotiations and that it was up to us to do our utmost to avoid any unwanted situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that paragraph you say that their assessment proved to be more correct because shortly afterwards a Serb policeman was killed. The Prosecution suggested to you that we - the Serbs - made use of that killing as an excuse to attack Rogatica. It was also suggested to you that Mr. Ujic on page 33459 said that there was some shooting and the use of artillery and so on and so forth. First of all, tell us this: Where did the murder take place and how far is it from the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: It's some 3 kilometres away towards Gorazde, to the south, where Bosnian -- Bosniak forces were in the area of Laze and Pasic Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say that it is not or that it is 3 kilometres away?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: It is 3 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was the fighting and where were mortars used?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: In that part when the territory was being liberated in order to pull out the dead man's body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In lines 21 and 22, I will read them out to you in English. [In English] "Of course there was an exchange of fire and the war was on its way." [Interpretation] That is page 33459, Ujic. So what is your position? Was it the Serbs who were firing unilaterally or is what Ujic said true, that there was an exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I think there was an exchange of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 51 of today's transcript you were asked, or rather, what was suggested to you was that we had taken advantage of that incident and the killing of the Serb policeman in order to take over Rogatica. When was Rogatica liberated?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I think it was sometime towards the end of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the meantime who was in Rogatica and who controlled the centre of town, the town itself, if you will?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: At first it was no one. After all, it was no man's land and probably it was both that were wandering around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you to look at a few documents. P3265, could we have a look at that, please. Please, Mr. Batinic, focus on this report of the battalion commander - it was a battalion at the time - of the Municipal Assembly of Rogatica of the 23rd of May and Kusic says there that they fired at an enemy stronghold, Dub, Pokrivenik, and Kozica and Cadovi ... and on Pasica Kula. And further down it says that: "The body of a soldier was recovered that had been in the possession of enemy forces for the last two day. There were no losses in the operations above Rogatica. In the rear the enemy forces killed two old men." So what does that mean "above Rogatica"? And does this report correspond to your own knowledge about this?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know much about this. I just know that the soldier, Mihajlovic, lost his life and that for about two days they could not get ahold of his body, then there was an exchange of fire, then Mihajlovic was taken out, and I don't know about these further reports and I couldn't really comment on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what this means, enemy stronghold Dub, Pokrivenik, and then further on Kopljevici, Kozica, Cadovi?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: In that area, that's where Muslim forces were stationed in the Muslim police. And then a family was killed there, Obradovic, three or four of them were killed brutally so that area towards Ustipraca and Gorazde was primarily under the control of the Bosniak forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 2 the witness said "brutally," "zverski" but maybe it's better to say "bestially."

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The learned Ms. Gustafson asked you today what it meant that you protected only villages that had expressed their loyalty. What about the other villages? Could you protect the civilians in those villages too that had not expressed their loyalty and what does loyalty or disloyalty consist of?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, I would prefer to say that it was Bosniaks, Muslims, who were the citizens in those villages. As for the other villages, we could not access them. That was within the war operations zone. The villages that we reached were accessible and they were not in the war zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I now please ask for 65 ter 7088. Please do focus on this regular operative report of the 29th of May, Commander Rajko Kusic sent it and says under number 2: "In the areas of Pokrivenik and Dub there are considerable enemy forces. About 3.000 to 4 -- or rather, 300 to 400 armed men are around Karacici, Golubovici and Vragolovi." What is that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: These are villages around the urban part of Rogatica. The population is predominantly Muslim and probably other people from certain villages who were there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 5 it says that they went to Ferizovici, and on the previous day the enemy operated against our positions in the area. What does that mean? Did the attacks come from Ferizovici?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: These were neighbouring villages. Ferizovici is predominantly Serb populated, and Vragolovi and the rest are Muslim-populated villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's now activated. All you asked about this document is some names of the places. Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness didn't appear to confirm any of the contents of the document, just the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- locations, so I don't think the foundation is there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, Your Excellencies, I asked on the basis of the questions put during the cross-examination in terms of why they did not protect civilians in Muslim villages. And it turned out that these villages had been taken by the Muslim army and they were actually firing from Ferizovici and this document shows that there was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are not giving evidence yourself. You did not ask a substantive question at all to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were asked about these villages, why you did not protect them. The content of this document, is it something that you're familiar with? Is it true that the enemy army was in those villages and it was firing from those villages.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this document but I know that these villages are around the urban part of town and these villages were primarily Muslim-populated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were there any Muslim fighters in these villages, any Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Probably, but I cannot confirm with 100 per cent certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Around these villages and between those villages and Serb villages, was there any fighting?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I cannot confirm that with certainty. It is certain that these villages were in a war zone at the time. There was always a bit of gun-fire. Where and how I cannot say because I was not a participant in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If this is not sufficient for you, I am going to tender this through someone else who is more familiar with the fighting. You decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think again the witness doesn't confirm the contents in it and Dr. Karadzic's suggestion is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, since you said so, tender it with another witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. But in relation to what had been asked and suggested during the cross-examination, I do have to get an answer from the witness in terms of whether civilians were being brought in and whether there was fighting. 65 ter 7543, could I have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, did you have any information about these civilians being brought in to town against their own will?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any shelling of Muslim settlements with the aim of driving the civilians out?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The second sentence now, please. If you have a problem with your eyesight: "Large numbers of Muslim civilians arrive in town every day, mostly women and children and unarmed people. The people are finding shelter in the secondary school centre. "Snipers are firing from two or three places in town. The enemy attacked a column ..." Et cetera, et cetera. These civilians, were they brought forcibly or did they flee from the fighting and did they come voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: There was certainly fighting in town and it is certain that civilians were trying to save themselves. I don't know what was going on there, but if somebody told them to go to the secondary school and that that was a safe place, then they probably went to the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Batinic, how do you explain this, that the Muslim civilians are seeking shelter from fighting in the Serb-held area of Rogatica? What kind of confidence is that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: It is certainly true that I would have welcomed that and I would want civilians and helpless people to be given shelter during all that fighting, and also I would want them to have appropriate accommodation. I believe that people -- a large number of people cannot stay in such facilities for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the one-but-last: "The following were used in operations in town: 350 x 7.62 mm bullets for the automatic rifle and semi-automatic rifle, 430 x 7.9 mm bullets and 520 bullets for the M84 light machine-gun. No shells were used."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not catch the question or the answer either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, the interpreters could not hear you because you were overlapping with the interpretation. Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be honest, I'm not very knowledgeable about weapons and I don't know whether that is a lot or a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question wasn't recorded either. I asked whether this was a large amount of ammunition that was used in urban warfare without shells?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I think it's not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again, the witness has basically speculated on the questions that have been put to him. He's made it clear he wasn't in the town at this time and wasn't even there until the operation -- until he says it was safe to go to the town at the end of July. He wasn't involved in any of these operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it -- you touched upon this issue, i.e., the situation in which the Muslim civilians were arriving and maybe ending up in the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did. Firstly, the document I put to the witness was a document addressed to him, it was also dated November 1992 after the witness had visited the secondary school. I'm not objecting to the questions; I'm objecting to the admission of this document because the witness wasn't in the town at this time, he wasn't involved in the operations in the town, and he hasn't been able to confirm the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. -- just a second. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. At the end of page 74 the witness said there was certainly fighting in the town. If you look at the fourth paragraph -- the fifth paragraph of the document it talks about their operations in the town. So he's confirmed that -- he's confirmed part of the document and I think that that's enough for the standard that you've been applying for and the arguments as to what he knew and how he knew it all go to weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2933, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us just note that this report is dated the 11th of June, and now let us call up 65 ter 7272.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked, Mr. Batinic, whether there had been fighting, whether we had attacked, whether we had attacked with the objective of expelling the Muslim population, and now I would like to ask you to take a look at this report of the 12th of June. The first sentence says: "In the area of the municipality the enemy became obvious in several places by infiltrating sabotage groups whose probable objective was creating a space for penetration and for linking forces in the interior with the forces in Zepa." We haven't got a translation yet. This was also written by Rajko Kusic and he sent it to the command of the Army of Republika Srpska. Further down it says: "A larger concentration of Muslim population has been noticed in town and they are staying in the secondary school centre. Among the population there are primarily women and children and there are also unarmed men. In town sniper shooters were also noticed and they were firing at town as the column was passing towards town, or rather, towards Gorazde." You were asked about civilians, about bringing in civilians. This report, is it correct according to what you know about the fighting and the way in which the civilians came into town?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: There were certainly groups that were armed on both sides and certainly there were wounded and dead persons in town. But, as this report says - and believe me, I cannot fully understand it. I was not authorised then. This is the first time that I see it. It is a fact that there was fighting in town, people were getting killed, and people were basically fleeing to places that were supposed to be safer for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the actual occurrence rather than the document, does this correspond to your own knowledge about the way in which civilians came to town and about the fighting -- actually, the level of conflict, or rather, presence of conflict, not level of conflict?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was certainly fighting for at least two months until late July when one could enter town finally, when we found those civilians in the high school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think there's any basis to admit it now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I will skip a few other documents in that regard. Could we next have -- I will not tender it. Let's look at 65 ter 7951. It is an analysis of combat-readiness until the 31st of December, 1992. 65 ter 7951. Page 3, please. There is a translation, apologies, that is why I didn't want to tender it. It has been translated. I wasn't aware of it. The last sentence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we have page 3 as well in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "In the village of Trnovo" the bottom of that page, in the Serbian the bottom of page 3. "Family" -- well, the next page, please. Obradovic, the Obradovic family, is that the family mentioned?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the line below "at the time," which is some ten lines from the bottom. The encircled Ustasha in the town --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's find the passage in the English as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think it's on the bottom half of page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: At that time ..." [Interpretation] The tenth line from the bottom in the [In English] "... encircled Ustashas ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "At that time, the encircled Ustashas started strategy Serb property and liquidating Serbs in town. In order to prevent this, the brigade had to intervene promptly in protecting the undamaged property and rescuing and saving those Serbs who were still alive." Is this the period in late July when Rogatica was liberated?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the truthfulness of the following paragraph. "Part of the enemy forces withdrew towards Kukavice ..." What is it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: It's a large Muslim-populated village in the direction of Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Part of enemy forces withdrew towards Kukavice leaving their families who have been taken care of and transferred to Sarajevo upon their wish." Is it correct that Muslim fighters left their families behind to the Serbs and that you took care of them and transported them to Sarajevo as they wished?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: The families were in the high school building in Rogatica and if they were armed, the men probably didn't dare to surrender and were probably planning to go to Lukavica and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think this has been already admitted as P2830, according to the e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well, yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Batinic, do you know of any investigation which established that Mr. Kusic had committed a crime?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you come to suffer on the 30th of November?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: That day I was visiting Burati village trying to arrange a delivery of food that they needed. I was there that day, and on the way back I came upon an anti-armour -- anti-tank mine. I was seriously injured and my work ability was seriously impaired at the time. After a lengthy recovery I engaged in the work that I was later busy with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whose mine was it, Mr. Batinic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I think some did not like the fact that I was visiting the area. I call it an enemy mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any information from Mustafa or from anyone else you knew in the villages that were under your protection, protection of the Serbian authorities, about the presence of their enemy soldiers and about your position concerning the peaceful villages?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, these people were quite good and honourable. We visited them frequently. The police went there often as well. They were in a state of fear, though. Even if they were visited by them, they didn't dare discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know General Asim Hodzic in person? For the participants, he was Muslim and a retired JNA general.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I knew him personally and I visited him frequently and provided food for him. When he fell ill we transferred him to the military medical academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did you see him last?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I think in 1993, early 1993, when he became ill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question, Mr. Batinic, did you and the people as a whole follow conferences about Bosnia and Herzegovina? In particular did they follow the publication of maps and what was the position of the inhabitants regarding the fate of their settlements?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Well, towards the end we definitely did. Irrespective of what opinion we had in Rogatica municipality, there was some reformist forces there as well from the movement for Yugoslavia. We rejoiced over any solution in order to further the goals of those conferences, starting with the Vance-Owen Plan in -- and the final discussion at Pale about the Vance-Owen Plan. To tell you the truth, I expected that your signature you placed in Athens would be acknowledged and confirmed but it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you this: If a village realised that it fell in one or other entity during a conference, would that have an impact or did it have an impact on the sentiment of inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. But it was up to the authorities to do their job so that everyone could feel comfortable wherever they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was suggested to you that I promoted Mr. Kusic because he had committed crimes and ethnically cleansed the population. Did you know what my position was regarding civilian population, especially minority population?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I think on one occasion I received a letter from you where you asked us and suggested to us that we should treat the rest of the population as we treat the Serbian population. I see no reason why you would reward someone for committing crimes. It would be irrational.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to draw your attention to D95 and D96 because it was mentioned by Mr. Batinic. The last question, Mr. Batinic, regarding the Crisis Staff. Before the municipal Crisis Staff was formed did the party have its own and why would it have been expanded in April?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: The party had its Crisis Staff comprising some ten people. Perhaps at the time they couldn't get their bearings right, but despite the pressure they were under, especially in Rogatica when there was no communication or links with the Main Board of the SDS and the Presidency of Republika Srpska, we still tried to come up with a solution in order to get out of this new situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. While the Crisis Staff was still party staff, did it have the authority as if it had executive remit?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was suggested to you that still the Serbian Municipal Assembly in Rogatica worked from the start, it was operational. It was shown that there was one session when it was set up and another one on the 15th of April. Did the Serbian Assembly of Rogatica municipality carry out its authority, irrespective of the fact how often it met?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: No, not until the Assembly session when the members of the Executive Board were elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when was it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: I don't recall it exactly when the Executive Board was elected, but there must be a document somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it before May or on the 2nd of May, as you said?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV BATINIC
utterances.text: Possible. I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Batinic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Batinic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of this Chamber I'd like to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- thank you for your coming to The Hague. Now you're free to go. Have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue there are a few matters I'd like to deal with. First, Mr. Robinson, with respect to the Defence request for state representative to be present in courtroom regarding Ambassador Jose Cutileiro's evidence, the Chamber would like to inquire with you whether the request for the two Portuguese representatives to be present in the courtroom during that testimony came from the Portuguese government or from Ambassador Cutileiro himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It came from Ambassador Cutileiro himself. It originated from him, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But could you clarify with the Portuguese embassy. It is their request or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I -- we also received a request from them. The first suggestion was made by Ambassador Cutileiro in a form that he filled out, and then they communicated to us that they would like to be present. So I -- unless you would like me to clarify further, I think that they would like to be present and it's at his request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So in accordance with the consistent practice of this Chamber, the Chamber would like you to file all correspond relating to this request.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the Chamber will now issue an oral ruling. On the 31st of January, 2013, during the direct examination of Witness Srdjan Sehovac, the accused presented Sehovac with a collection of four transcripts of intercepted conversations bearing 65 ter number 1D6136. Sehovac testified that as head of the SNB Ilidza department, "all documents had to pass through my hands." He described the process of interception by the operatives under his oversight and further commented on the meaning and content of the intercepts. The Office of the Prosecutor objected on the ground that admission of the intercept on such a showing would dilute the Chamber's standards for authenticating intercepts and that Sehovac's statements were less comprehensive than those of Witness KDZ145, who was not personally involved in intercepting conversation but provided lengthy description of SDB intercept operations and thus authenticated intercepts during the Prosecution case. The Chamber marked the intercepts for identification as MFI D2853. At the conclusion of Sehovac's testimony, upon further inquiry from the Chamber, Sehovac described in more detailed the process of intercepting conversations, including the location of the relevant tapes and the fact that he listened to most of the conversations himself. The Chamber reiterates its consistent approach to authentication of intercepts and recalls that one method of doing so is through the testimony of an intercept operator. The Chamber considers that Sehovac's testimony about his direct involvement in the interception and its reporting process, including the fact that he listened to many personally is sufficient for the purpose of authenticating this intercept in this manner. The Chamber thus will admit MFI D2853 into evidence. And finally, having reviewed the Rule 92 ter notification and statement for Tomislav Savkic, the Chamber finds that the last sentence of paragraph 62 and the document referred to therein and the last sentence of paragraph 81 contain excessive detail about specific crimes committed against Bosnian Serbs which is not relevant to the charges against the accused in the indictment and orders that they be redacted. Unless there's any other matter -- yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we will need a longer-than-customary break between -- in order to set up for the next witness. As the Trial Chamber may be aware, Ms. Sutherland is here despite a recent disability and that creates a couple of logistical issues to take care of that require a brief recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, and just one administrative matter that arose in the last few moments of the witness's evidence. Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic mentioned Exhibit D95 which I then looked up and I noted that it is the same document as the associated exhibit which was -- which was admitted as D2932 through the witness. And I was wondering if D2932 should be vacated given that it's already in evidence as D95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That was 65 ter 17452, referenced at paragraph 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think we can vacate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do so. Ten minutes would be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll rise for ten minutes. --- Break taken at 2.11 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Savkic. Do you hear me in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Before you start giving evidence, Mr. Savkic, I'd like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the accused, the Prosecution, or the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt for a criminal offence or could provide that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer that question. But in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony which was compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Savkic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you [In English], Your Excellency, for your pronunciation of our impossible names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Savkic.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC
utterances.text: God be with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have to ask you that we both pause and that annunciate our sentences slowly so they could all be recorded in the transcript. Did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 1D7213 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the statement on the screen in front of you? Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read it and signed it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page, please. So can we identify the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Here and there there may be a thing or two that is different from the way I talk, but the essence is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you want to change something? Are you talking about the choice of words?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC
utterances.text: Well, some things haven't been explained. Look at 99. I don't see how I missed that, 99, paragraph 99, the first line, the second line, the third line -- actually, it's the second line. It says: "The instances of one side exacting revenge from the other are well-known to have taken place in Zaklopaca, Zutica, Kravica, Glogova, or destruction of the Vlasenica mosque after Serb civilians of the Kljestani and Sadici villages had been burned and massacred." And now there's a part that's missing. On the very next day family members or friends or whoever destroyed it. That part is missing. As for the rest, basically it will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I suggest the following wording then or, for example, the destruction of the mosque in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was destroyed by members of the family or friends?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of the persons who were killed in Kljestani and Sadici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Bjelovac, does it remain there because it does say Bjelovac and other places?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's all right. Well, Bjelovac is particularly well-known.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything else that should be changed?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV SAVKIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, no. Terminologically, well, in one place, for instance -- now, I cannot -- well, it should be in the plural. It should say buses went to get the Muslims in Zalazje and it just says "bus" here, but let's say that this is a question of grammar -- well, it's not the same thing, is it, if one bus goes or if several buses go because one bus can take some 50 military conscripts and then in two buses there's over a hundred, so the number drastically changes, the number of persons who were transported from Zaljonica [phoen] Vlasenica.

utterances.text: Bravo, yes, that's it. As far as I know there were two buses from Rogatica and two from Vlasenica, so there were four as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

utterances.text: Before I hear from the Prosecution whether it has any objection, I have several matters with respect to some of the associated exhibits.
